title: Vega allows calling it faith’s certainty if not equated with catholic dogmatic certainty
source_text: XLIV. Neque tamen illi ipsi Scholae Romanae Doctores qui certitudinem istam nolunt dici fidei divinae, multum repugnant quin nomen istud ei tribuatur, modo non aequiparetur certitudini fidei illius quam Catholicam & dogmaticam vocant. Id videre est apud Vegam, qui concedit propter Ecclesiae pacem hanc certitudinem posse commodo sensu certitudinem fidei appellari, quia a fide divina bona ex parte profluit; & ad eam fides mediate concurrit, & qui certi sunt de sua justitia, certitudinis ejus bonam partem fidei debent. Nisi enim, inquit, per fidem assentirentur illis majoribus illis propositionibus de fide, Facienti quod in se est Deus non denegat gratiam; Convertens se ad Deum toto corde, invenit & obtinet gratiam ipsius, Nunquam illi certitudinem aliquam haberent de sua gratia, &c. Additque per fidem sciri posse, An simus in gratia; neque id negare Conc. Tridentinum, sed tantum negare sciri hoc posse certitudine fidei: nimirum haec duo distinguit, scire per fidem, &, scire certitudine fidei; Et prius hic vult habere locum, non vero posterius, juxta Conc. Tridentini mentem. In Conc. Trident. decret. de Justif. lib. 9. cap. 47.
pass_a_gloss: Nor nevertheless do those very doctors of the Roman School who refuse to have that certainty called of divine faith much resist that that name be attributed to it, provided it is not equated with the certainty of that faith which they call Catholic and dogmatic. That is to be seen in Vega, who concedes that for the Church’s peace this certainty can in a fitting sense be called certainty of faith, because it flows in good part from divine faith; and faith mediately concurs to it, and those who are certain of their righteousness owe a good part of that certainty to faith. For unless, he says, through faith they assented to those major propositions of faith—To the one doing what is in him God does not deny grace; Turning himself to God with whole heart, he finds and obtains his grace—they would never have any certainty concerning their grace, &c. And he adds that through faith it can be known whether we are in grace; nor does the Tridentine Council deny that, but only denies that this can be known by certainty of faith: namely he distinguishes these two, to know through faith, and to know by certainty of faith; And he wants the former to have place here, not the latter, according to the mind of the Tridentine Council. In Conc. Trident. decret. de Justif. lib. 9. cap. 47.
pass_b_english: Vega softens the label: call it faith’s certainty if you refuse equality with catholic dogma.
Trent (on his reading) blocks ‘certainty of faith,’ not every knowing ‘through faith.’
